passages.t: Baasha's house falls the way Jeroboam's did
passages.happening:
The word of the LORD comes to the prophet Jehu son of Hanani against Baasha: “Even though I lifted you out of the dust and made you ruler over My people Israel, you have walked in the way of Jeroboam” (verse 2). So Baasha's house will end as Jeroboam's did (verses 3-4). Baasha dies and is buried in Tirzah, and his son Elah reigns (verse 6). The narrator adds that the word came against Baasha for all his evil, ‘and also because Baasha had struck down the house of Jeroboam’ (verse 7).

Elah reigns two years. While he is drinking himself drunk in the house of his steward in Tirzah, his servant Zimri, commander of half his chariots, plots against him, kills him, and takes the throne (verses 8-10). At once Zimri strikes down Baasha's whole household, every male, kinsman or friend, ‘according to the word that the LORD had spoken against Baasha through Jehu the prophet’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The northern kingdom's instability reaches a low point: three kings in quick succession, two of them murdered, and then a civil war. Baasha reigned about 909 to 886 BC, Elah about 886 to 885.

To be lifted out of the dust is a picture of being raised from low rank, as in Hannah's song. The phrase reminds Baasha that his throne was a gift he had forgotten.

When one ruling house replaced another, it was common to kill every male of the old royal house to prevent revenge or rival claims, and here it reaches kinsmen and friends. The text records it as the fulfillment of a prophet's word, and it does not hold it up as right. The idols of verse 13 are called worthless, in Hebrew hevel, breath or vapor, the word that opens Ecclesiastes: as empty as a breath and unable to do anything for those who worship them.

The verb for Zimri's plotting, qashar, to conspire, marks the north's recurring way of seizing power. Baasha had done the same to Nadab.
passages.later: Hannah had sung of the God who ‘raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap’ (1 Samuel 2:8). Isaiah asks of a power that God used as his tool and then judged, ‘Does an axe raise itself above the one who swings it?’ (Isaiah 10:15).
passages.hard:
If Baasha fulfilled God's word by destroying Jeroboam's house, why is he condemned for it (verse 7)?

The tension is real, since Ahijah had announced that destruction (14:10-14). Most interpreters answer that Baasha acted from his own ambition, not in obedience to any command, and that he then repeated the very sins for which Jeroboam's house fell. God used his violence to carry out a judgment, but that did not make Baasha righteous.

The prophet Hosea later speaks the same way of Jehu's bloodshed at Jezreel. The principle, found elsewhere too, as in Isaiah's words about Assyria, is that God can use a sinful agent to accomplish a just purpose while still holding that agent accountable for his motives and his methods.
passages.asks: Baasha was raised from the dust and forgot who raised him. Ask what gift you have come to treat as your own achievement. And ask whether you have ever done a right thing for a wrong reason, and called it obedience.

passages.t: Seven days, a civil war, and Omri
passages.happening:
‘In the twenty-seventh year of Asa’s reign over Judah, Zimri reigned in Tirzah for seven days’ (verse 15). The army is besieging Gibbethon, and when the soldiers hear what Zimri has done, they make Omri, the commander of the army, king that same day (verse 16). Omri marches on Tirzah and besieges it. When Zimri sees that the city is taken, he takes his own life in the palace (verses 17-18). He dies for his sins, for he walked in the way of Jeroboam (verse 19).

The people are divided: half follow Tibni son of Ginath, and half follow Omri. Omri's side proves stronger, Tibni dies, and Omri reigns (verses 21-22). He reigns twelve years, six of them in Tirzah (verse 23). “He bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver and built a city there, calling it Samaria after the name of Shemer, who had owned the hill” (verse 24). ‘But Omri did evil in the sight of the LORD and acted more wickedly than all who were before him’ (verse 25). He dies, is buried in Samaria, and his son Ahab reigns (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
Zimri reigned seven days in 885 BC. The dates the text gives show that the civil war with Tibni lasted about four years, from Asa's twenty-seventh year to his thirty-first. Omri reigned about 885 to 874 BC.

Out of the chaos comes the house of Omri, the most powerful dynasty the north would have. Omri is the first Israelite king named in sources outside the Bible. The Mesha Stele, a Moabite inscription of the ninth century, says that he humbled Moab for many days, and Assyrian records went on calling Israel the house of Omri long after his line had ended. His new capital, Samaria, stood on a hill with commanding views, and excavations there have found a royal quarter of fine masonry and many carved ivories.

Yet the narrator gives Omri a few verses and a harsh verdict. The book cares about faithfulness more than about power.
passages.later: Micah, more than a century later, still names this house as the pattern of Israel's failure: ‘You have kept the statutes of Omri and all the practices of Ahab’s house’ (Micah 6:16).
passages.hard:
Zimri took his own life. How does the Bible treat this?

The text reports it in a single sentence and without comment, and these notes do not dwell on it. The Bible records a few such deaths, among them Saul's, Ahithophel's, Zimri's and Judas's, and each is told as the tragic end of a life that had gone badly wrong. The Bible never presents taking one's own life as a good or honorable way out.

Scripture holds that human life belongs to God and that no one is beyond his mercy. Zimri's story is the end of a man trapped by what he had done. The Bible's story does not end in despair, and help is there for anyone in that kind of darkness.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Omri was the strongest king the north had, and Scripture gives him a few lines. Ask what God measures in a life that the world does not. And ask what you are building, as Omri built Samaria, that will outlast you, and what it will be remembered for.

passages.t: Ahab, Jezebel, and a temple for Baal
passages.happening:
‘In the thirty-eighth year of Asa’s reign over Judah, Ahab son of Omri became king of Israel, and he reigned in Samaria twenty-two years’ (verse 29). He does evil in the sight of the LORD, more than all before him (verse 30). As if the sins of Jeroboam were not enough, ‘he even married Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians, and he then proceeded to serve and worship Baal’ (verse 31). He sets up an altar for Baal in the temple of Baal he built in Samaria, and an Asherah pole. ‘Thus Ahab did more to provoke the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger than all the kings of Israel before him’ (verse 33).

“In Ahab’s days, Hiel the Bethelite rebuilt Jericho. At the cost of Abiram his firstborn he laid its foundation, and at the cost of Segub his youngest he set up its gates, according to the word that the LORD had spoken through Joshua son of Nun” (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
Ahab reigned about 874 to 853 BC. He appears in the Kurkh Monolith of the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III, which lists him with a large force of chariots in a coalition that fought the Assyrians at Qarqar in 853 BC. Kings mentions none of this, a sign of how selective its interests are. Ethbaal was a king of the Phoenician coast, and the marriage sealed an alliance with the trading cities.

Baal, whose name means lord or master, was the Canaanite storm god, the rider of the clouds who brought rain and fertility. In texts from Ugarit he dies and comes back to life, and his return was linked to the coming of the rains. For farmers in a land that depended wholly on seasonal rain, his worship made practical sense, which is why it tempted Israel so long. Asherah was a goddess worshiped beside him. Ahab's temple of Baal in the capital made this worship royal policy. With Ahab the danger is no longer only Jeroboam's calves, which were at least meant for the LORD, but the open worship of another god.

The verse about Jericho seems to stand alone, but it shows that the LORD's word, even a word spoken centuries before through Joshua, still comes true. It prepares for the next verse, where Elijah appears.
passages.later: Joshua had laid the curse on Jericho: “Cursed before the LORD is the man who rises up and rebuilds this city, Jericho; at the cost of his firstborn he will lay its foundations; at the cost of his youngest he will set up its gates” (Joshua 6:26).
passages.hard:
What happened to Hiel's sons?

The text says only that the rebuilding cost Hiel his firstborn and his youngest, as Joshua had said. Some interpreters think the sons died as a direct judgment. Others suggest that Hiel offered them as sacrifices at the laying of the foundation and the setting of the gates, a practice some scholars think was known in the region, though the evidence for it is disputed. The text does not decide, and these notes do not dwell on it.

On either reading, the verse does not call what happened good. It sets the deaths in the days of Ahab, the king who had turned Israel to Baal, as a sign that the LORD's word stands.

A word for anyone who was not protected by a parent, or was handed over to harm by someone who should have kept them safe. This story does not call that right. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. If you are still in danger, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ahab married into Baal's worship and built it a temple in his capital. Ask what you have let in through an alliance that you would never have chosen for its own sake. And ask whether you treat God's word as old and spent, as Hiel did, or as a word that still stands.
